rationale: ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner and protocol, so the connectivity features are shifted per site. Scoring is within site, so I'll z-score every connectivity feature within its own site before the classifier. The site means come from the training items, or from the test items when a site has no training data, which uses no labels. This lets the L2 logistic regression learn ADHD-vs-control differences inside each site instead of differences between sites.

I'm replacing the Pearson correlation with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance on CC200, mapped into the Riemannian tangent space at the group geometric mean. Raw correlations treat matrix entries as independent Euclidean values, even though covariance matrices are curved (positive-definite). In large rs-fMRI benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019), the tangent embedding was the most reliable connectivity measure for linear classifiers. Shrinkage also stabilises sites with short scans (fewer timepoints than ROIs) and ROIs that are all zeros. The reference mean is label-free.

I'm changing the model from a single CC200 classifier to an average over four atlases (CC200, AAL, Harvard-Oxford, Talairach). Each atlas gets the same pipeline: Ledoit-Wolf tangent-space features, per-site z-scoring, and its own L2 logistic regression. The idea is that ADHD's connectivity signal is weak and noisy, and different parcellations make different, partly independent errors. Averaging their predictions should reduce variance, and multi-atlas ensembles have helped in ABIDE/ADHD-200 benchmarks. Each regression's C is scaled by its feature count (C = 0.001 × 20100 / p), so the smaller atlases are regularized about as strongly per feature as the CC200 model. I haven't run this, so its score isn't known yet.

Instead of mapping every subject to the tangent space at a single global mean, I'll re-centre each site at its own log-Euclidean mean covariance. Site means come from training items, or from that site's test items if the site has no training data. Each site's covariances are whitened so its mean becomes the identity, then log-mapped. Scanner and protocol differences act multiplicatively on covariance matrices, so this Riemannian re-centring (Zanini et al. 2018) should remove the site effect at the matrix level, which z-scoring after a shared tangent map can't do. Per-site z-scoring and the L2 logistic regression stay the same.

Right now each ROI's time series is z-scored before the covariance is estimated, so the regional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation is thrown away. Altered ALFF in frontal, striatal and default-mode regions is a well-replicated ADHD marker (Zang et al. 2007). I'll add a 200-feature block of log relative ALFF per ROI, centred on each subject's mean over ROIs so scanner gain cancels. The block is site-standardized with the tangent features and up-weighted so it carries the same total variance as the ~20k connectivity features, which acts like an equal-weight sum of two linear kernels. I haven't run this, so its score isn't known yet.

Use the training labels to make each site's reference statistics class-balanced. For both the Riemannian re-centring and the per-site z-scoring, the centre becomes the average of the control and ADHD class means instead of the plain site mean, and the scale becomes the pooled within-class SD. ADHD-200 sites have very different ADHD prevalence, so a plain site mean is pulled toward whichever class dominates that site. That shifts cases and controls differently at each site and mixes the true ADHD signal with the site's case mix. Balancing removes that bias. It uses training labels only, inside `fit_predict`. Sites with only one class, or no training data, fall back to the existing label-free statistics.

The L2 strength (C=0.001) is a fixed guess, but in a regime with about 20k features and about 700 subjects, the right shrinkage depends on how weak the ADHD signal is. I'll choose C for each training fold by an inner 3-fold grouped CV that reruns the whole label-aware site re-centring and standardization inside each inner fold. The selection criterion is the same within-site AUROC the harness uses. The pipeline itself is unchanged, and I haven't run this yet.

Each training subject will get a sample weight so that, within every site, the ADHD and control classes carry equal total weight and the site keeps its overall size. With C=0.001 the logistic weights come out roughly as the label-weighted sum of the features. With uneven case mixes across sites, that sum mixes the within-site ADHD-vs-control difference with leftover offsets between sites. Balancing the classes inside each site makes the learned direction close to the size-weighted average of within-site class differences, which is what the within-site AUROC measures.

I'm switching the parcellation from CC200 to the finer CC400 atlas (about 392 ROIs) and keeping the rest of the pipeline as is. ADHD connectivity changes are thought to be small and spread across fronto-striatal, default-mode and attention circuits. Coarse parcels average signals together, which can cancel those effects. Large connectome benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019; Abraham et al. 2017) also found that finer parcellations with tangent embedding and strong L2 tend to classify slightly better. To keep the effective L2 strength the same, C is scaled by 20100 divided by the new feature count. I also changed the storage to keep memory down: float32 features, and covariances unpacked one subject at a time.

The current model keeps the global signal, which Athena never removed, and that shared component can swamp the weak ADHD signal. I'll add a second CC400 view computed after regressing each subject's global signal out of every ROI, and average its normalized logistic score with the current model's (no global-signal regression). The two kinds of connectome carry partly different information, so averaging should cut the variance of this weak-signal classifier without throwing away what the current model may learn from the global signal (including real motion differences between ADHD and control children).

Moving from CC200 to CC400 was the largest single gain (+0.022). That suggests the ADHD connectivity signal depends on parcel resolution, so the two resolutions probably make partly independent errors. Round 3's multi-atlas average was diluted by weaker atlases (AAL, Harvard-Oxford, Talairach). This round I'll average only the two Craddock resolutions, CC400 and CC200. Each runs through the current pipeline unchanged, and each model's score is scaled by its spread on the training set before the two are averaged.

Some subjects have ROIs that are all zeros because those regions fell outside the scan's field of view, and this is probably more common with CC400's small parcels. Right now those subjects get artificial covariance rows (a shrinkage-only diagonal and zero coupling), which turn into large outliers in the tangent space. With strong L2 the logistic weights are roughly a label-weighted sum of features, so those outliers add noise to the weights. They also inflate the per-site pooled SD. The fix fills the missing ROIs' rows and columns in two steps. In `featurize`, they get the population-average connectivity, computed without labels. In `fit_predict`, they are replaced by the site's re-centring reference before whitening, so missing data sits at "no deviation" rather than looking like strong connectivity changes. Each filled matrix is projected back to positive definite, with an eigenvalue floor set by the subject's observed block.

I'm changing what each subject's covariance is shrunk towards. Right now Ledoit-Wolf shrinks it towards the identity; this round it shrinks towards its site's population-mean correlation, with the subject's own Ledoit-Wolf-optimal intensity (a PoSCE-style prior, Rahim et al. 2019). ADHD-200 scans are often shorter than the 392 CC400 ROIs (OHSU has about 78 timepoints), so the identity target pulls noisy subjects towards a matrix far from the site mean the tangent map is taken at. A population prior instead damps each subject's deviation towards the reference, which should give cleaner tangent features. It is not run yet, so there is no score.

I'm adding a low-rank denoising step to the classifier weights. ADHD connectivity changes are thought to sit in a few large-scale networks (default-mode, fronto-parietal, attention, striatal), so the true discriminative pattern over the 392×392 ROIs should be close to low rank. With strong L2, the logistic weights are roughly a noisy class-difference map over about 77k features. The change refolds those weights into a symmetric ROI×ROI matrix and keeps only the eigencomponents that stand above the random-noise level. That level comes from a robust estimate of the per-entry noise, with no tuning; if no component clears it, the original weights are kept. Each kept eigenvalue is also shrunk to remove its expected noise inflation, and this projection should remove much of the estimation noise.

This round only changes the noise threshold used in the low-rank weight denoising. The current threshold assumes the weight errors are independent from entry to entry (a random-matrix edge estimated from the spread of the weight entries). But connectivity features that share an ROI are strongly correlated, so the weight noise is itself structured, and its top eigenvalues can sit well away from that assumed edge. I'll measure the edge directly instead: refit the same weighted logistic regression on training labels shuffled within each site (8 shuffles, which keeps each site's case mix and weights). The edge becomes the mean of the largest absolute eigenvalue across those shuffled fits. Only components that clear this null level are kept and shrunk as before.

I'm changing only the eigenvalue shrinker in the low-rank weight denoising. Right now each kept component is shrunk to its de-biased signal eigenvalue θ, but in the spiked-Wigner model a component near the noise edge also has a noisy eigenvector: its squared overlap with the true one is only 1 − σ²n/θ². So I'll use the Frobenius-optimal shrinker η = θ·(1 − σ²n/θ²) = θ − edge²/(4θ), which should damp weak components more and cut reconstruction error. It falls continuously to zero at the edge, so there's no hard on/off jump, and it adds no new hyperparameters. I haven't run it, so there's no score yet.

Each site's per-feature SDs are estimated from only about 30–80 training subjects over roughly 77k tangent features. Dividing by these noisy SDs re-weights the features differently and at random for each site's test subjects. A noisy site mean only shifts all scores in a site together, which within-site AUROC ignores, but noisy scaling does not cancel out that way. So I'll add ComBat-style empirical-Bayes shrinkage of the scale. Each site's log-SD is modelled as a site offset plus a feature profile shared across sites plus a residual. The residual is shrunk with a factor set by moments: (true residual variance) / (true variance + sampling variance 1/(2·dof)). This has no tuned hyperparameters; sites with only one class and sites with no training data still use the old fallback.

With C=0.001 the logistic weights are close to a class-difference sum over subjects, so a few training subjects with very large tangent-space deviations (likely motion or registration artifacts, common in children with ADHD) dominate both the weight estimate and the test scores. I'll divide each subject's site-standardized feature vector by its own RMS (a spatial-sign normalization) before the global standardization. Every subject then has the same influence on the estimated direction. Test subjects are scored on the direction of their connectivity deviation, not on its overall size.

Ledoit-Wolf picks its shrinkage on the assumption that fMRI timepoints are independent. The Athena data are band-passed to below 0.08 Hz at a TR of about 2 s, so neighbouring timepoints are strongly autocorrelated. The sample covariance is therefore 2–4× noisier than LW thinks, and LW shrinks too little. With 392 ROIs and scans of about 80–260 frames, the leftover noisy small eigenvalues become large, random terms in the log, and those dominate the tangent features. This change multiplies each subject's LW shrinkage by a Bartlett variance-inflation factor, f = 1 + 2·Σₖ ρ̄(k)², capped at a shrinkage of 1. ρ̄(k) is the subject's ROI-averaged autocorrelation at lag k. The fix uses no labels and adds no new hyperparameters. I haven't run it, so it has no score yet.

I'm adding DVARS-based censoring of motion spikes ("scrubbing") before each subject's Ledoit-Wolf covariance is estimated. The data give no motion estimates, so I'm using DVARS as a stand-in; DVARS is the RMS change in the per-ROI z-scored signal from one frame to the next. A frame counts as an outlier when its DVARS is more than 3 robust SDs (from the median absolute deviation) above the subject's median. Each outlier is removed together with one frame before and one after it, and no more than 25% of a subject's frames are removed. Head-motion bursts in children inflate connectivity in a way that has nothing to do with the brain (Power et al. 2012), and those artifacts add large random deviations to the tangent features. This change is label-free, only touches subjects with real spikes, and leaves the rest of the pipeline unchanged. I haven't run it, so its score isn't known yet.
